headings.title: Introduction to Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
headings.content: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) represent a major public health challenge globally, and particularly within Nigeria, where young adults and vulnerable populations bear a disproportionate burden of disease. As student nurses, understanding the foundational epidemiology, transmission routes, and psychosocial impacts of STIs is crucial for providing holistic and non-judgmental care. STIs are caused by various bacterial, viral, protozoal, and fungal pathogens transmitted predominantly through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral intercourse, as well as vertically from mother to child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Beyond immediate physical symptoms such as urethral discharge, genital ulcers, or pelvic pain, untreated STIs can lead to severe long-term complications including pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, infertility, and increased susceptibility to HIV transmission. In the Nigerian healthcare context, nurses frequently encounter patients presenting with advanced complications due to delayed health-seeking behavior, cultural stigma, and financial barriers. Therefore, mastering STI prevention and control is not merely about treating a disease, but about advocating for sexual health education, empowering communities, and dismantling stigmas that hinder early diagnosis and treatment. By approaching STI care with clinical competence, empathy, and cultural awareness, nursing professionals play an indispensable role in interrupting chains of transmission and improving maternal and child health outcomes across healthcare facilities in Nigeria.

headings.title: Common Pathogens and Transmission Dynamics
headings.content: Sexually transmitted infections are caused by a diverse group of microorganisms, each with unique transmission dynamics and clinical manifestations. Bacterial pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Treponema pallidum (the causative agent of syphilis) are typically curable with appropriate antibiotic therapy, though rising antimicrobial resistance poses a significant clinical threat in Nigerian healthcare settings. Viral pathogens, including Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Human Papillomavirus (HPV), establish lifelong infections that require lifelong management, suppression, or specific vaccination strategies. Protozoal infections like Trichomonas vaginalis also contribute significantly to the global burden of curable STIs. Transmission dynamics are heavily influenced by biological factors—such as mucosal disruption and coinfections that increase viral shedding—as well as behavioral and social determinants like concurrent sexual partnerships, low condom use, and limited healthcare access. Pathogens often exploit microscopic abrasions in the mucosal membranes of the reproductive and gastrointestinal tracts during sexual acts to gain entry into the host. Understanding these transmission dynamics allows nurses to identify high-risk populations, anticipate specific clinical presentations, and tailor targeted health education interventions to break the cycle of infection within communities.

headings.title: Primary Prevention Strategies and Safe Sex Practices
headings.content: Primary prevention strategies form the bedrock of public health initiatives aimed at reducing the incidence of sexually transmitted infections. These strategies focus on intercepting infections before they occur by promoting safe sex practices, modifying high-risk behaviors, and empowering individuals with accurate health information. Consistent and correct use of barrier methods, particularly male and female latex condoms, remains the single most effective intervention for preventing the sexual transmission of HIV and other bacterial and viral STIs. Nurses must skillfully educate patients on proper condom application, storage, and disposal, while also dispelling common cultural myths. Beyond barrier methods, primary prevention encompasses behavioral counseling strategies such as promoting mutual monogamy, reducing the number of sexual partners, and encouraging open communication between partners regarding sexual history and STI status. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) also play critical roles in primary and secondary prevention frameworks for specific populations at high risk for HIV. In community and clinical settings across Nigeria, nurses are uniquely positioned to conduct outreach, distribute educational materials, and provide non-judgmental counseling that normalizes safe sex practices, thereby fostering a culture of proactive sexual health and wellness.

headings.title: The Role of Vaccinations in STI Prevention
headings.content: Immunization is a powerful primary prevention tool that has revolutionized the control of specific viral sexually transmitted infections. Vaccines currently available target viral agents that have significant morbidity and mortality, most notably Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV). HPV vaccination is highly effective in preventing persistent infections with high-risk oncogenic types (such as types 16 and 18) that are responsible for the vast majority of cervical, anal, and other anogenital cancers, as well as low-risk types that cause genital warts. In Nigeria and globally, public health programs increasingly target adolescent girls and boys before the onset of sexual activity to maximize vaccine efficacy. Similarly, the Hepatitis B vaccine is a cornerstone of immunization schedules, protecting against a blood-borne and sexually transmitted virus that causes chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. As healthcare professionals, student nurses must understand vaccine schedules, storage requirements, and the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy within communities. Nurses play an essential role in advocating for national immunization policies, educating parents and adolescents on the safety and efficacy of these vaccines, and administering doses correctly to build robust community immunity against vaccine-preventable STIs.

headings.title: Screening, Early Detection, and Diagnostic Testing
headings.content: Screening, early detection, and diagnostic testing are vital components of secondary prevention, allowing for prompt treatment, interruption of transmission chains, and prevention of long-term sequelae. Many STIs, particularly chlamydia, gonorrhea, and early syphilis, are frequently asymptomatic, especially in women, making clinical examination alone insufficient for diagnosis. Consequently, routine screening protocols are recommended for high-risk populations, pregnant women, and sexually active adolescents. Diagnostic modalities vary depending on the pathogen and local resource availability; they include nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)—which are the gold standard for sensitivity and specificity using urine or swab samples—serological blood tests for syphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis, and point-of-care (POC) rapid diagnostic tests that provide immediate results in resource-limited or remote Nigerian clinical settings. Student nurses must be proficient in collecting accurate clinical specimens (such as endocervical, urethral, or pharyngeal swabs), maintaining patient confidentiality, and interpreting diagnostic reports. Furthermore, nurses must provide compassionate pre- and post-test counseling, ensuring patients understand the implications of their test results, manage anxiety, and adhere strictly to follow-up care and treatment regimens once results are confirmed.

headings.title: Clinical Management and Treatment Protocols
headings.content: Clinical management and treatment protocols for STIs are guided by standardized, evidence-based guidelines developed by health authorities to ensure prompt cure, prevent complications, and combat antimicrobial resistance. Bacterial infections are treated with specific antibiotic regimens—such as single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone combined with oral azithromycin for gonorrhea, or benzathine penicillin G for syphilis. It is imperative that healthcare providers adhere to syndromic management protocols where laboratory testing is unavailable, treating patients based on recognized constellations of symptoms (e.g., vaginal discharge or urethral discharge syndromes) to ensure immediate intervention before patients are lost to follow-up. Patient education during treatment must emphasize complete adherence to prescribed medication regimens, even if symptoms resolve quickly. Furthermore, nurses must instruct patients to abstain from sexual intercourse for at least seven days following the completion of treatment and until all sexual partners are successfully treated to prevent reinfection. Management must also address the psychological impact of a diagnosis, provide guidance on managing side effects of medications, and schedule appropriate test-of-cure evaluations when indicated, particularly for pregnant women or complex presentations.

headings.title: Partner Notification and Contact Tracing
headings.content: Partner notification and contact tracing are critical public health interventions designed to break the cycle of STI transmission within communities. When an individual is diagnosed with an STI, identifying, notifying, and treating their sexual partners is essential to prevent reinfection, protect the health of partners who may be unaware of their exposure, and curb community spread. There are two primary methods of partner notification: patient referral, where the index patient takes the responsibility of informing their partners, and provider referral, where trained public health personnel or nurses confidentially contact partners without disclosing the index patient's identity. In Nigeria, cultural sensitivities, fear of domestic violence, and intense social stigma surrounding STIs can make partner notification extremely challenging. Consequently, nurses must approach contact tracing with high levels of cultural competence, confidentiality, empathy, and safety assessment. Nurses educate index patients on how to communicate with partners, offer assistance with partner notification letters or expedited partner therapy (EPT) where legally and clinically appropriate, and ensure that all identified contacts receive prompt diagnostic evaluation, counseling, and treatment.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions, Patient Education, and Counseling
headings.content: Nursing interventions, patient education, and counseling are the cornerstones of comprehensive STI care, requiring a delicate balance of clinical expertise and interpersonal skill. Nurses serve as educators, advocates, and direct care providers who must create a safe, confidential, and non-judgmental environment for patients seeking sexual health services. Educational counseling should cover correct condom use, the importance of adherence to pharmacological treatments, risk reduction strategies, and the necessity of screening and partner treatment. Because STIs are frequently associated with intense societal stigma, anxiety, and relationship discord—particularly in conservative or patriarchal settings—nurses must employ therapeutic communication techniques, active listening, and trauma-informed care. Empowering patients involves discussing bodily autonomy, negotiating safer sex with partners, and providing information on available community resources. Furthermore, nurses must advocate for policy changes, destigmatization of sexual health services in Nigerian hospitals, and comprehensive sexuality education in schools and communities. By integrating compassionate counseling into everyday nursing practice, nurses ensure that patients feel respected, informed, and supported throughout their healthcare journey.
